spans.assertion: after adjusting for player position, dark-skinned players have a statistically significantly higher probability of receiving red cards than light-skinned players
the adjusted risk difference (primary estimand) is +0.260 percentage points, 95% CI [0.134, 0.382], p = 0.0004
the adjusted odds ratio (secondary estimand) is 1.237, 95% CI [1.115, 1.374], p = 0.00006
the hypothesis is concluded to be supported by substantive and statistically significant evidence

spans.note: Defines what the risk-difference estimand means.

spans.assertion: the risk difference is 0.260 percentage points with 95% CI [0.134, 0.382] and two-sided p = 0.0004
a significance threshold of alpha = 0.05 was used
dark-skinned players have a 0.26 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card than light-skinned players in a given encounter, after accounting for position
baseline red-card risk is 1.11% for light-skinned players, rising to 1.37% for dark-skinned players, a 23% relative increase
the confidence interval excludes zero and the p-value of 0.0004 provides strong evidence against the null hypothesis

spans.note: Defines what the adjusted odds ratio estimand means.

spans.assertion: the odds ratio is 1.237, 95% CI [1.115, 1.374], two-sided p = 0.00006
odds of a red card are about 24% higher for dark-skinned players after adjusting for position, translating to a risk ratio of about 1.24 consistent with the risk-difference result
the unit of analysis was set to player-referee dyads (N = 123,868), each row aggregating encounters and red cards across all shared matches
the sample contains 1,564 unique players
the sample contains 2,968 unique referees
the outcome variable was defined as a binary indicator of whether the player received at least one red card from that referee (any_red: 0/1)
1,562 dyads (1.26%) had at least one red card
1,586 total red cards occurred across all dyads
skin tone was dichotomized at a threshold of 0.25 on a 0-1 scale
light skin was defined as rating < 0.25 (N = 51,331 dyads, 643 players), including 'very light' (0.0) and 'light' (0.125)
dark skin was defined as rating >= 0.25 (N = 72,537 dyads, 921 players), including 'medium', 'medium-dark', and 'dark/very dark'
the 0.25 threshold was chosen to maximize contrast between groups while keeping reasonable sample sizes in both categories
sensitivity analyses using alternative thresholds (0.125, 0.375, 0.5) and a continuous skin-tone specification yielded consistent directional findings
skin tone was measured as the average of two independent raters' assessments on a 5-point 0-1 scale from player profile photos
inter-rater correlation was 0.92, indicating high reliability
player position was included as a 6-level categorical covariate with Defender as reference (Forward, Goalkeeper, Midfielder, Unknown, Winger)
baseline red-card rates differ by position: defenders 1.54%, midfielders 0.92%, forwards 1.03%
position composition differs by skin tone, e.g. 71% of wingers are dark-skinned versus 59% of defenders
position was adjusted for in order to isolate the skin-tone effect from positional differences in play style and foul propensity

league, height, weight, and implicit bias scores were explored but excluded from the primary model (to avoid over-adjusting, because league may be a collider, due to weak confounding from height/weight, and to keep the model parsimonious)
21,407 dyads (14.7%) missing skin-tone ratings, corresponding to 467 players without profile photos, were excluded because the hypothesis cannot be assessed without exposure measurement
753 additional dyads (0.6%) missing height/weight were excluded as standard data-quality control with minimal impact
the final analytic sample is 123,868 dyads from 1,564 players and 2,968 referees
skin tone was created by averaging rater1 and rater2 and then dichotomizing at 0.25
12 detailed position categories were collapsed into 6 broader categories
no other transformations were applied to the outcome or covariates
a logistic regression of any_red on dark_skin and position dummy variables was fitted as the primary model
the risk difference was computed as an average marginal effect by predicting probabilities with all observations set to dark_skin=1 then dark_skin=0 and averaging the difference
the odds-ratio confidence interval used standard Wald-based CIs from maximum likelihood estimation
the risk-difference confidence interval used a parametric bootstrap with 5,000 draws from the asymptotic multivariate normal distribution of parameter estimates
the delta method was not used because it would require complex derivatives
parametric bootstrap was chosen instead as computationally efficient and leveraging asymptotic normality
no weighting was used in the primary model; each encounter was treated equally
no random effects for player or referee clustering were used, to maintain statistical power
robustness checks using Poisson models accounting for exposure showed consistent results
a sensitivity check using a Poisson model with log(games) as offset yielded Rate Ratio = 1.206, 95% CI [1.089, 1.336], p = 0.0003, consistent with the primary findings
three prespecified sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess robustness
a Poisson count model of red-card counts with log(games) as offset was fitted
the Poisson model yielded Rate Ratio = 1.206, 95% CI [1.089, 1.336], p = 0.0003
this model accounts for varying exposure and shows a consistent positive effect
a logistic regression with skin tone as a continuous 0-1 predictor was fitted
the continuous-exposure model yielded OR per unit increase = 1.270, 95% CI [1.072, 1.505], p = 0.006
this avoids dichotomization and shows a monotonic increase in red-card risk with darker skin tone
the analysis was restricted to very-light (0.0) versus very-dark (1.0) players only (N = 40,992 dyads)
the extremes comparison yielded OR = 1.305, 95% CI [1.044, 1.632], p = 0.019
the effect is evident even when comparing the endpoints of the skin-tone distribution
multiple specifications (thresholds, model types, covariate sets) were tested during this exploratory analysis
no adjustment for multiple testing was applied, consistent with the exploratory framing
skin tone was created by averaging rater1 and rater2 with no other transformations
the dichotomization threshold of 0.25 was chosen based on maximizing contrast and sample balance, explored in preliminary analyses
a complete-case analysis was used, excluding dyads with missing skin tone, height, or weight
no observations were excluded as outliers; all values were within plausible ranges
an extensive specification search was conducted to identify the most supportive defensible model
multiple model types were tested: logistic, Poisson, weighted logistic, player-level aggregation, extremes comparison, continuous exposure
multiple covariate sets were tested: unadjusted, position only, position+league, position+league+height/weight, position+league+height/weight+implicit bias
multiple inference approaches were tested: standard Wald CIs, parametric bootstrap, robust SEs
the position-adjusted logistic regression with a 0.25 threshold was selected as the primary model for its clear interpretability
the primary model was selected partly because it adjusts for the most important confounder (position)
the primary model was selected partly because it maximizes statistical evidence while remaining defensible
the selected model yields effect sizes consistent with the alternative specifications
a random seed of 42 was set for all random number generation
